extracted.intended_audience: new patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) responding to USPTO office actions
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, stepwise guidance for preparing a response to a first office action at the USPTO, covering how to read rejections, map claim elements to references, choose between argument and amendment, tone, use of claim charts, examiner interviews, and after-final options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the rejection three times before doing anything
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the Office Action three times: first for emotional reaction; second ignoring tone and identify which claims are rejected under which sections (101, 102, 103, 112); third with the cited references open to compare what they actually disclose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First read: acknowledge your emotional reaction so it doesn't drive your drafting. Second read: objectively map which claims are rejected and under what statutory grounds (101, 102, 103, 112). Third read: open the cited references and verify whether the examiner's factual citations actually teach the claimed elements — many office actions that seem 'bad' are defensible once you check the references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map every claim element to every cited reference
rubrics_metrics.description: For a 103 rejection, build a literal table: rows are claim elements, columns are references, and cells are the passages cited by the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Populate the table with the exact passages cited. This reveals (a) elements where the cited passage does not teach what the examiner asserts and (b) elements with no citation at all — both are valid bases for argument. Use the chart as an evidence-focused tool to identify weaknesses in the examiner's combination or factual assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh argument versus amendment strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the trade-off: arguing without amending preserves claim scope but risks more file-history estoppel if you later amend; amending without argument concedes the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a combined approach when strong: make a narrow amendment to address the examiner's point and include a clear argument explaining why the amended language is not taught or suggested by the references. Be mindful that unnecessary amendment concedes patentably indistinct subject matter and that pure argument may fail to persuade and later limit you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disparaging the reference; use neutral, precise tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't write attacks like 'the examiner clearly misunderstands the reference' or 'this rejection has no basis.' Instead, precisely cite what the reference discloses and what it is silent about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame criticisms as factual comparisons: e.g., 'the cited passage at column 4, lines 13-22, discloses X but is silent as to Y.' Maintain professional tone; personal attacks or inflammatory language invite a final rejection and reduce persuasive force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include claim charts in the response
rubrics_metrics.description: Although not required, include a one-page claim chart for the amended independent claim to make the examiner's job easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concise claim chart clarifying where each claim element is located (or not) in the prior art dramatically increases odds of allowance. Keep it to one page for clarity and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when to call the examiner (conduct an interview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Schedule a 15-minute interview after a first office action — it's usually free, often results in agreed-upon language, and can save a round of correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your amendment is non-trivial, call before filing the response to discuss and try to reach agreement on claim language. Short interviews can yield mutually acceptable solutions and prevent unnecessary amendment or appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for after-final options and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: After a final rejection, options narrow: you can file an RCE (expensive, restarts examination), an after-final response, an AFCP 2.0 request, or a pre-appeal brief — choose before drafting your response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the timing and consequences of each post-final avenue (cost, procedural effect, likelihood of success). Selecting the right post-final strategy early informs how aggressively to argue or amend in your pre-final response.
